messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Ricardo's Story

Ricardo Morales had spent forty-two years prosecuting violent crimes, building a reputation as a meticulous and unflinching advocate for victims. At sixty-seven, he had secured countless convictions, testified before juries with the precise authority of a man who had trained himself to speak only facts, and maintained a carefully constructed distance between his professional certainty and his inner life. That distance collapsed three years ago, on a spring evening when he stayed late at the courthouse to review case files. A colleague—someone he had worked alongside for nearly a decade—cornered him in the empty records room, overpowered him, and sexually assaulted him. Ricardo had been unable to stop it. His body, which he had always regarded as an instrument of his will, had failed him entirely.

In the months that followed, Ricardo began to notice people he had known for years in a new and terrifying light. His younger brother's visits became sources of acute dread; the presence of his brother's children in his home triggered a cascade of intrusive images so vivid and overwhelming that he found himself making excuses to avoid family gatherings altogether. What frightened him most was not just the memories themselves but what they revealed: that the world contained hidden dangers in the faces of people he thought he knew, that trust was a luxury he could no longer afford. He had come to believe his body was permanently compromised, that something essential in him had been destroyed and could never be restored. The violation had marked him in ways he was certain others could sense—a contamination that clung to him despite countless showers, a fundamental wrongness that no amount of professional success could erase.

The intrusive memories arrived without warning and with devastating clarity. When his hand brushed against cool tile in his kitchen—a temperature identical to the surface he had been pressed against during the assault—the memory did not simply return; it seized him entirely. He was back in that records room, the smell of paper and fluorescent light overwhelming his senses, the weight of another body pinning him down. The memory felt present, not past, a current reality that his rational mind could not override. Each time this happened, it reinforced his conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that his body was irrevocably damaged, that people who appeared trustworthy harbored violent intentions. These appraisals, once formed, began to reshape how he moved through space. He found himself scanning for exits the moment he entered any room—a habit so automatic now that he barely registered doing it. He noticed potential weapons everywhere: letter openers on desks, the sharp edge of a picture frame, the weight of a paperweight that could be used to inflict harm. His threat detection had become hypervigilant and exhausting.

As the months progressed, Ricardo began to avoid unfamiliar places entirely. He could not assess danger in environments he did not know, could not predict where threats might emerge, could not control the variables. This avoidance narrowed his world significantly. He stopped attending professional conferences, declined invitations to restaurants he had never visited, and increasingly confined himself to the familiar geography of his home and his office. Yet even these refuges offered no real safety. The memory of his colleague's face—someone he had walked past in hallways hundreds of times—would surface unbidden, and with it came a renewed sense that people close to him, people within his inner circle, posed the greatest threat. He began to withdraw from his brother, from his few remaining friends, from any situation where he might encounter someone unexpected or be reminded of his vulnerability. The prosecutor who had spent decades protecting others now felt utterly unprotected, his body a betrayed vessel, his mind a prison of unwanted recollection, his carefully ordered life contracting into smaller and smaller safe zones that no longer felt safe at all. It was only when his supervisor expressed concern about his declining courtroom presence and his increasing isolation that Ricardo finally acknowledged he could not continue this way alone.
